use: Often someone's history: kako no koto (what happened before).

example.romaji: kako no koto wa mou ii yo.
example.ja: 過去のことはもういいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kako no koto wa mou ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 過去のことはもういいです。

notes: For 'long ago', mukashi is often more natural.

use: A bit formal; in chat people mostly say kore kara.

example.english: Be more careful from now on.

examplePolite.english: I'll be more careful from now on.

notes: kongo tomo yoroshiku onegai shimasu is a set business sign-off.

use: After a past-form verb: mita shunkan (the moment I saw it).

example.ja: 顔見た瞬間、わかったよ。
example.english: I knew the moment I saw his face.

examplePolite.ja: 顔を見た瞬間、わかりました。
examplePolite.english: I knew the instant I saw his face.

use: A little formal; in chat people usually say mae.

example.romaji: izen koko de hataraiteta n da.
example.ja: 以前ここで働いてたんだ。

examplePolite.ja: 以前ここで働いていました。

notes: X izen = X or earlier: sanji izen (by three).

use: Mostly as kurou suru (to struggle, have a hard time).

example.romaji: heya sagashi, kekkou kurou shita yo.
example.ja: 部屋探し、結構苦労したよ。
example.english: Finding an apartment was a real struggle.

examplePolite.romaji: heya sagashi ni wa kekkou kurou shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋探しには結構苦労しました。
examplePolite.english: I had quite a hard time finding an apartment.

notes: gokurousama = thanks for your hard work, said to staff or juniors.

use: A memory you keep, not the ability to remember.

example.ja: いい思い出になったね。
example.english: That turned into a great memory.

examplePolite.ja: いい思い出になりました。

use: Polite; in chat people say kono aida.

example.ja: 先日はお世話になりました。
example.english: Thank you for your help the other day.

use: Sounds formal, as on forms, news and announcements; in chat say ima.

example.romaji: genzai no juusho, koko ni kaite ne.
example.ja: 現在の住所、ここに書いてね。

examplePolite.romaji: genzai no juusho o koko ni kaite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 現在の住所をここに書いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please write your current address here.
